I served on the energy subcommittee when he chaired that. And I counted a privilege to have served with him. But people have asked, do you take the same stands and votes as Fred? And my answer is no, not all the time, very clearly. Fred had a different district to represent. I represented the seventh district which was a swing district and R plus one, R plus two district that we talk about. In political speak, campaign speak, it was truly swing district. This new district is a very conservative district, solid Republican district. That is very easy for me to represent because I think my conservative ideals are exactly with the new district. But I would tell them that I'm going to work with people across the aisle to try to accomplish things because I'll need that. But I also know, in most cases, what the red line is that I can't cross. And that gives me an opportunity to go up that red line if I have to and to get something accomplished that we need to move forward. That's doable. But they can assume that my record will still be conservative, strongly conservative, based upon the principles that really were the foundation of the Republican Party in now the fifth district, Jackson, Michigan, 1854, under the Oaks, July 6, the Emancipation Party, which was the Republican Party was formed under the ideals that people deserve freedom and opportunity. regardless of race creed color. As long as we espouse the American ideals and move forward, everybody ought to have the opportunity to move the direction they want to move and experience success. And when they fail, we don't kick them. We reach out of hand, pick them up, pat them on the back and say, let's get back at it. So that'll be my ideal as I represent the fifth district.

explicit_propositions.text: I served with Fred Upton on the Energy and Commerce Committee for fourteen years.
My voting positions are not always aligned with Fred Upton's.
Fred Upton chaired the Energy Subcommittee during my service on it.
The current district I represent is a very conservative, solid Republican district.
Fred represented a different congressional district than I did.
My conservative ideals align closely with those of my current district.
I previously represented Michigan's 7th District, which was a swing district (R+1 to R+2).
I considered it a privilege to serve with Fred Upton.
I recognize specific limits—'red lines'—that I cannot cross in negotiations.
I intend to work across the aisle to achieve legislative outcomes.

assumptions.text: Legislators should adapt their policy positions based on the ideological makeup of their constituency.
A representative’s core values should remain consistent even when electoral districts change.
Conservative ideology is best defined by principles of individual liberty, opportunity, and merit-based success.
The Republican Party’s founding ideals centered on racial equality and universal opportunity.
Political compromise requires knowing where one’s non-negotiable boundaries lie.
Electoral district characteristics determine the legitimacy and necessity of shifting policy stances.
Supporters expect consistency in a representative’s party-aligned record over time.
People who fail should be supported rather than punished, reflecting a moral obligation of society.
Representatives should balance pragmatism with principled advocacy to deliver results.
Historical origins of political parties provide relevant ethical guidance for modern representation.
